cells.tense: Here, hands on it — you're tending what you chose, and you know you chose it.
cells.ask: Say to yourself, before the day gets loud, which of the two of you the next hour is actually for.
cells.core:
You picked this, and you're still picking it, which is most of it. What you're growing gets real attention — you read what it needs, you give that, and you're not running yourself ragged doing it. Some seasons it goes smooth and some it doesn't; neither one changes what you're doing.

The momentum you feel didn't come from deciding it ought to work. It came from being in it — you're in contact with the person and you're carrying the load, and both are happening at once. Look at what's already taken shape instead of what you hope shows up. Name the thing the next hour is for, and let that be enough.

cells.tense: Already out past today, in a version where you know how this ends and you're tending it from there.
cells.ask: Describe what's actually here today, out loud, then leave the picture of how it ought to be alone for the afternoon.
cells.core:
You're tending a version that hasn't arrived. The picture of how it should look finished is getting your care ahead of what's here — ahead of what either of you has said. It can feel like devotion. Part of it is grip, and the grip is spending the thing it's trying to protect.

When this is working, the growing happens without you hauling it: you hold the space and you don't clutch, and the thing gets to be small and unfinished in front of you. What you're growing doesn't need more planning. It needs you in the room where it actually is.

Stand beside the real thing today, in this hour, and let the finished picture wait.

cells.tense: Back at a door you shut behind you and haven't walked through since.
cells.ask: Tell one person one true thing about what you'd want this to become — in your own words, in their hearing.
cells.core:
Not much is being tended right now. What you'd want to grow is still there, and saying it out loud isn't happening. The care didn't leave; the offering to anyone did.

This one is usually quieter when it's working. You can tell what's yours from what isn't without needing an argument, you're fine not having it settled, and you say the small true thing before you're sure. That's still in you — it just isn't getting used.

Say one plain true sentence to one person about what you'd want it to become. Not a plan, not a case. It doesn't have to be someone who can give you anything back.

cells.tense: Already writing, with the pen set down.
cells.ask: Put one line on paper — for nobody — naming what you've been tending, and leave it where you'll see it in the morning.
cells.core:
What comes next with someone is already being shaped by you — when you stay, what you leave alone, what you say — and when it comes up it sounds like the situation, or patience, or just how it is. The care is doing real work in the room. Nobody has put a name on whose it is.

This looks different when it's working: the small practice doesn't need force behind it, and the solitude connects instead of cutting off. Your own aim here is simpler than the explaining. Do the small thing in front of you, admit the care is the point, and let the day show whether it holds.

Naming it isn't taking credit in front of another person. It's turning the pen back to the hand that's been holding it, which is something you can do at this table.

attempts.check: The one unsupported personal claim a draft tends to make here is that the connection has already been chosen and is being hidden — the record says only that authorship of tending has gone unclaimed, so the cell hedges to what is being done rather than what has been privately decided. A reader could reasonably say the merging hasn't happened at all and nothing is being tended, which is why the Too Little cell runs on the closed door and the seat staying empty rather than on any claim about another person. Every ask survives being wrong: the asking-one-question, standing-back, and writing-it-down acts return something usable even if the reading misses, and none of them promises a fix. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is any line announcing that the tending is 'really' a choice already made — cut it; the cell only says the acting-as-if is running.
